course.description: A 14-week course on design-based inference from complex samples: from total survey error through sampling designs, weights and calibration to design-based variance estimation and reproducible analysis in R.
outcomes: Decompose survey error and identify which components a design addresses
Compute inclusion probabilities and base weights for SRS, stratified, cluster, multistage and PPS designs
Apply and critique nonresponse adjustment, post-stratification, raking and calibration
Estimate design-based variances, design effects and effective sample sizes, and explain why iid formulas fail
Carry out and document a reproducible complex-survey analysis in R
course.audience: MA students in sociology, survey methodology or applied statistics; QDA2 or an equivalent inference course assumed.
course.workload: 1 × 90 min lecture + 1 × 90 min lab per week + ~3 h self-study
course.instructorNotes: Steps 1–12 of the Weighting Studio are spread over weeks 1–10; each week re-opens the same instrument with a different configuration. Never present SRS formulas for cluster samples without the deff qualification. Validate all lab numbers students report against R survey before grading.

variant.body:
In a probability sample every unit k of the population has a known, nonzero chance of being selected: its inclusion probability πₖ. The design fixes πₖ before any data are collected; it is not estimated from the sample.

The design (base) weight is dₖ = 1/πₖ. A respondent with πₖ = 1/50 stands for 50 population units. Under simple random sampling every πₖ = n/N, so all weights are equal and weighting changes nothing. Under a disproportionate stratified design, units in oversampled strata have larger πₖ and therefore smaller weights.

Weights correct for the unequal selection probabilities that the design itself created. On their own they cannot repair coverage error or nonresponse.

variant.prompt: Before you open the lab: the sample below takes the same number of people from each education group, although the tertiary group is only a fifth of the population and scores highest. Will the unweighted sample mean be above, below or close to the true population mean? Write your prediction and one reason.

variant.instructions: The design is fixed: a stratified sample of 120 with equal allocation, so the small tertiary group is oversampled. Select three sampled units from different groups and write down πₖ and dₖ = 1/πₖ for each. Then go to the Estimates stage and compare the unweighted, HT and Hájek means with Ȳ.

variant.body:
The Horvitz–Thompson estimator of the population total weights each sampled value by its design weight:

$$\hat{Y}_{HT} = \sum_{k \in s} \frac{y_k}{\pi_k} = \sum_{k \in s} d_k\, y_k$$

Dividing by the known population size N gives the HT mean. The Hájek estimator divides by the estimated population size, the sum of the weights, instead:

$$\bar{y}_{H} = \frac{\sum_{k \in s} d_k\, y_k}{\sum_{k \in s} d_k}$$

HT is exactly unbiased over repeated samples. Hájek is a ratio: approximately unbiased in large samples and usually more stable when the number of respondents is random (cluster designs, nonresponse). With equal weights both reduce to the ordinary sample mean.

config.expected: mean ≈ 5.43 with SE ≈ 0.18 and DEff ≈ 2.4; the unweighted mean is ≈ 5.48. Values from R 4.3.3 with the survey package on the same synthetic rows.

variant.prompt: Your R output reports a design-based SE and a design effect above 2. Explain in three sentences what the design-based SE takes into account that the naive s/√n does not, and when the two would coincide.

questionItems.prompt: Weights in a survey are w = (1, 1, 3, 3). What is the Kish effective sample size?

options.why: That is the nominal n; unequal weights reduce the effective n.
n_eff = (Σw)² / Σw² = 64 / 20 = 3.2, not the number of distinct weight values.

questionItems.explanation: n_eff = (Σw)²/Σw² = 8²/(1+1+9+9) = 64/20 = 3.2; the Kish deff is n/n_eff = 1.25.

b1e.body:
In a probability sample every unit k of the population has a known, nonzero chance of being selected: its inclusion probability πₖ. The design fixes πₖ before any data are collected; it is not estimated from the sample.

The design (base) weight is dₖ = 1/πₖ. A respondent with πₖ = 1/50 stands for 50 population units. Under simple random sampling every πₖ = n/N, so all weights are equal and weighting changes nothing. Under a disproportionate stratified design, units in oversampled strata have larger πₖ and therefore smaller weights.

Weights correct for the unequal selection probabilities that the design itself created. On their own they cannot repair coverage error or nonresponse.

conceptCards.def: First-order πₖ = P(k ∈ s); second-order πₖₗ for pairs, needed for exact variance. Determined entirely by the design.
misconceptions: πₖ is estimated from the sample
Equal πₖ implies SRS

conceptCards.def: dₖ = 1/πₖ: how many population units a sampled unit represents; base weights before any adjustment.
misconceptions: Weights fix nonresponse bias by themselves
SPSS WEIGHT BY gives correct SEs

b1h.body:
The Horvitz–Thompson estimator of the population total weights each sampled value by its design weight:

$$\hat{Y}_{HT} = \sum_{k \in s} \frac{y_k}{\pi_k} = \sum_{k \in s} d_k\, y_k$$

Dividing by the known population size N gives the HT mean. The Hájek estimator divides by the estimated population size, the sum of the weights, instead:

$$\bar{y}_{H} = \frac{\sum_{k \in s} d_k\, y_k}{\sum_{k \in s} d_k}$$

HT is exactly unbiased over repeated samples. Hájek is a ratio: approximately unbiased in large samples and usually more stable when the number of respondents is random (cluster designs, nonresponse). With equal weights both reduce to the ordinary sample mean.

conceptCards.def: Design-unbiased estimator of a total: sum of yₖ/πₖ over the sample. Its variance uses second-order probabilities.
misconceptions: HT is also the natural estimator of a mean (the Hájek ratio usually is)

conceptCards.def: Mean estimated as weighted sum of y divided by sum of weights; slightly biased, usually much less variable than HT/N.
misconceptions: Dividing by N and by Σd gives the same estimate

title.en: R: a weighted estimate with svydesign

b1i.objective: Declare the stratified-cluster design and compute the design-based mean, SE and deff; compare with the Complex Survey Lab.

config.code:
library(survey)
# trust_survey is injected from the Dataset block (synthetic; 3 strata × 4 PSUs × 15)
des <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~weight, data = trust_survey)

svymean(~trust, des, deff = TRUE)
mean(trust_survey$trust)          # unweighted, for comparison
confint(svymean(~trust, des))
config.expected: mean ≈ 5.43 with SE ≈ 0.18 and DEff ≈ 2.4; the unweighted mean is ≈ 5.48. Values from R 4.3.3 with the survey package on the same synthetic rows.
